messages.author: 3ea57457192f4f3b
messages.subject: devtools and github dependencies
parts:
I was wondering if anyone has done some work on implementing a system for resolving dependencies that are on Github? As more packages these days are not on CRAN, this problem gets increasingly pressing. I'd really like to add support for this in OpenCPU, one way or another.

Before I start hacking on something myself, I was wondering if any of the 144 forks (?!) has already done something.

messages.author: 7f0257cd1389289f
messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
parts: Dear Jeroen,

On 21 Dec 2013, at 06:52, Jeroen Ooms wrote:

I was wondering if anyone has done some work on implementing a system for resolving dependencies that are on Github? As more packages these days are not on CRAN, this problem gets increasingly pressing. I'd really like to add support for this in OpenCPU, one way or another.

Before I start hacking on something myself, I was wondering if any of the 144 forks (?!) has already done something.

I haven't done anything and I am not aware of particularly relevant work from anyone else. But, I do agree that there is a need to be met here. I had wondered whether this might just as well be achieved by a sort of metapackage website that gathered together information for both CRAN/bioconductor packages as well as in development R packages on github, rforge etc.

Recently I was thinking about what search it would take to find R packages on github automatically – something about repos containing a DESCRIPTION file in their root folder that can be read in by read.dcf etc. Then I happened to notice this:

https://github.com/hadley/r-on-github

So perhaps that could be a source of the location of packages not available on cran/bioc.

Best wishes,

Greg.

messages.author: 3ea57457192f4f3b
messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
parts:
On Sun, Dec 22, 2013 at 3:15 AM, Gregory Jefferis <jeff...@gmail.com> wrote:
 by a sort of metapackage website that gathered together information for both CRAN/bioconductor packages as well as in development R packages on github, rforge etc...... Then I happened to notice this: https://github.com/hadley/r-on-github. So perhaps that could be a source of the location of packages not available on cran/bioc.

I doubt this provides reliable foundations for resolving dependencies. You're going to get package name collisions because github does not enforce unique repo names as do cran/bioc. On the contrary: github encourages forking and branching, so there are many versions of one and the same package. I think we should try to support that, rather than inheriting limitations from the cran system. 

In my paper in the R journal (http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2013-1/ooms.pdf) I tried to make a case for versioning dependencies. I think we can hit 2 birds with 1 stone by using the github user-repo-branch system. For example, we could introduce some optional file in the source package accompanying the DESCRIPTION file (say: DEPENDENCIES), containing something like (dcf format):

Package: MASS
Version: 7.3-22
URL: http://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/MASS/MASS_7.3-22.tar.gz

Package: ggplot2
Version: 0.8.9
URL: https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/archive/ggplot2-0.8.9.tar.gz

Package: dplyr
Version: *
URL: https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/archive/master.tar.gz

The default R package manager could simply ignore this file and try to pull MASS, ggplot2 and dplyr from CRAN as defined in DESCRIPTION. But advanced package managers could use information in this file to locate dependencies more carefully, rather than assuming the latest version from cran. E.g. in devtools we can just feed the urls to devtools::install_url() before installing the main package.

The OpenCPU system already uses a separate library for every package installed form github to prevent package version conflicts. So if we could implement some system that resolves dependency packages from specific url/branch rather than cran, that could bring reproducibility a step closer. 

Let me know if this sounds sensible/doable/terrible :)

This is what packrat does for a project specific library (as well as
caching the source packages), but I think you need something more
proactive.

For packman, I was thinking of adding a source field that would work
something like this:

Sources@R: list(CRAN(), bioc(), github("hadley"), extrafont = github("wch"))

Packages would be installed from the first source that had the
requested version. I think this is relatively simple, and yet allows
sufficient flexibility. I don't think you want to leave the
DESCRIPTION file if at all possible.

messages.author: 3ea57457192f4f3b
messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
parts:
On Thu, Dec 26, 2013 at 2:26 PM, Hadley Wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Packages would be installed from the first source that had the
> requested version. I think this is relatively simple, and yet allows
> sufficient flexibility. I don't think you want to leave the
> DESCRIPTION file if at all possible.

I personally prefer using URI/URL over a custom syntax; The URL was
designed to solve exactly this problem of locating and identifying
resources, and is widely recognized and implemented. Also you don't
need an intermediate step repository index files (packages.rds, etc).
In the example you give, the package manager somehow needs to figure
out which R packages github user 'hadley' has available, which is not
trivial.

A URL points straight to the source, which is more simple and general.
Because systems like git are also based on the URL, you can directly
refer to any branch for any repo for any user on any server, without
making the system any more complex. This gives more flexibility, and
allows the user to cut out the repository gatekeepers. It would also
make it easier to write alternate package managers that support this
spec; downloading a file from a url is a lot easier than having a set
of predefine repositories (cran, bioc, github, etc), each with their
own indexing formats that need to be queried in order to see what is
available from where and how to get it.

You could still define shorthands for special cases, e.g. extrafont =
github("wch") is short for https://github.com/wch/extrafont/master.

messages.author: b756a7daa2c2aa6d
messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
parts:
> I personally prefer using URI/URL over a custom syntax; The URL was
> designed to solve exactly this problem of locating and identifying
> resources, and is widely recognized and implemented. Also you don't
> need an intermediate step repository index files (packages.rds, etc).
> In the example you give, the package manager somehow needs to figure
> out which R packages github user 'hadley' has available, which is not
> trivial.

Well just think of those functions as url shortcuts - you could
provide a url if you wanted, but most R packages will come from a
handful of places, so why not capture the most important sources with
some helper functions? The problem is a little easier than
determining what packages a github user provides, you only need to be
able to determine if they provide a specific package - and you can do
that with a single request.

> A URL points straight to the source, which is more simple and general.
> Because systems like git are also based on the URL, you can directly
> refer to any branch for any repo for any user on any server, without
> making the system any more complex.

But what url would you point to? The url to the page that represents
the branch? The url to the zipball? There's not an unambiguous url
that refers to any git repo + user + branch. And even if there was,
you might also need a url that has the package in a form that's easy
for R to get to. You can't assume that every use will have git
installed.

> This gives more flexibility, and
> allows the user to cut out the repository gatekeepers. It would also
> make it easier to write alternate package managers that support this
> spec; downloading a file from a url is a lot easier than having a set
> of predefine repositories (cran, bioc, github, etc), each with their
> own indexing formats that need to be queried in order to see what is
> available from where and how to get it.

Perhaps you could make that argument if we were starting from scratch,
but we're not, and any new system must be as easy to use as the
existing system for any of the main repos.

Hadley

--

> you only need to be able to determine if they provide a specific package - and you can do that with a single request.

How would this work? Suppose a package is installed with a dozen of
recursive dependencies, and Sources@R: list(github("hadley"),
github("yihui"), github("rstudio"). How is the package manager going
to decide where to get each package from? Will it have to query one by
one github/hadley/pkg, github/yihui/pkg and then github/rstudio/pkg to
try if it has a repo with a name identical to the package, for each
depencency package?

> But what url would you point to? The url to the page that represents
> the branch? The url to the zipball? There's not an unambiguous url
> that refers to any git repo + user + branch.

Fair enough, although an archive with the source package in it's root
(just as they are created by cmd build) seems to be pretty
conventional. We can easily figure out what kind of archive format it
is.

On Fri, Jan 10, 2014 at 2:54 PM, Hadley Wickham <h.wi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I agree it's nice to be able to use URLs, but they are verbose compared to:

You can still define shortcuts for special cases such as "github,
hadley, plyr, 1.8" ==>
https://github.com/hadley/plyr/archive/plyr-1.8.tar.gz. But that way
you don't become completely dependent on github.
> And urls do change over time.

I (strongly) disagree :) The "current" version of a certain package
on, say, CRAN is what changes over time. The resource
https://github.com/hadley/plyr/archive/plyr-1.8.tar.gz will be the
same; that's the entire point of git tags. Alternatively, a package
author can decide to host some dependency packages on his personal
homepage/webserver, and from there it is completely up him if the
dependencies are still there 10 years from now.

messages.subject: Re: devtools and github dependencies
parts:
Yes, that is a design flaw in CRAN. They should just put the file in their archive right away, and make a symlink or redirect from /src/contrib. A bit more modern/professional archives/repositories, whether it's Github or arxiv.org or JSS, make an effort to make sure URLs are preserved, because they know the URLS are used to lookup and identify their resources from places that might not easily be updated. (scripts, articles, search engines).

The URL provides a widely-used easy-to-implement syntax for providing a permanent link to a resource. Of course not every website does a good job, as is the case with everything. But the package author can decide to only use URLs from domains owned/managed by a trusted party. E.g. you could just use http://archive.had.co.nz/ggplot2_0.9.3.1.tar.gz.

See also this feature request on github:

https://github.com/hadley/devtools/issues/387

What we all seem to be after is a (modern) package management system that allows continued use of CRAN and other such repos.

It might be instructive to consider other package management suites. For example, homebrew (as far as I can tell), hosts recipes for installing packages in the form of ruby scripts on github repos. And it is possible to set up new "kegs" on github repos that are different to the main keg.
